places.title: A home in the walled city
places.sub: One family's flat, January 1987 · about 23 m² · six people
places.intro: One family's flat, as it might have looked in January 1987, the month the clearance was announced. It is about 23 m² (250 sq ft), the typical size reported for a unit in the city, and six people live here: parents, a grandmother and three children. The flat is not a record of one real home: the layout and almost every object are illustrative, typical of crowded Hong Kong homes of the time. Where former residents or reports describe homes in the walled city itself, the object says so, with its source.

voices.name: Former residents

voices.quote_en: In such terrible conditions, we had the best relationships.

voices.name: Ping (平哥)
voices.quote_zh: 我們當年在城寨好太平
voices.quote_en: In those years in the walled city we were very peaceful.
voices.summary: He came from Chaozhou as a teenager and opened a fish-ball factory in the city in the 1980s with HK$6,000. Rent and utilities came to under HK$2,000 a month, and no licence or tax was needed. Police patrolled two or three times a day and signed a book; when a neighbour lost power, the flat above lowered a plug. After the clearance he moved the business to Fuk Lo Tsun Road.
voices.source: Ming Pao Weekly (明周文化), 'Beyond the darkness: real memories of the walled city', by Leung Yi-kei, Tam Chi-wing and Wong Ka-pong, 13 June 2024

voices.name: Mr Ng (吳先生)
voices.quote_zh: 如果正常一隻窗，你係開唔到三分一
voices.quote_en: An ordinary window: you couldn't open even a third of it.
voices.summary: He moved in at four or five and lived there about ten years. Six of them shared a unit of roughly 100 sq ft with bunk beds, and rats ran along the beams. Before water reached the flats, families queued at street taps; later it came through unofficial connections. He spent time on the roofs, watching the planes come in.
voices.source: ACOO, 'Hong Kong corners: a tour with one of the walled city's last residents', by Hoiyan, May 2024

voices.name: Mr Yuen (袁先生)
voices.role: resident for more than ten years, on 龍津路
voices.quote_zh: 早走早著
voices.quote_en: Better to leave early.
voices.summary: He carried two buckets of water up nine floors. The building next door leaned against his flat, and he remembers children who fell from the roofs. When the clearance was announced his family decided to go early, and later moved into private housing.
voices.source: Inmedia (獨立媒體), report on an exhibition at Kowloon City Plaza, via Yahoo News Hong Kong, 24 May 2024

voices.quote_en: If I have the ability and the chance, I will leave this place.
voices.summary: His family of eight rented the upper floor of a two-storey tin-sheet house of about 400 sq ft, and the roof leaked whenever it rained. After primary school he assembled toys for pocket money; at twelve he left school to train as an electrician, and later worked in bakeries. He married in his early twenties and moved out in 1985.
voices.source: Ming Pao Weekly (明周文化), 'Beyond the darkness: real memories of the walled city', by Leung Yi-kei, Tam Chi-wing and Wong Ka-pong, 13 June 2024

voices.name: Maggie
voices.role: lived there three or four years after marrying Charles
voices.quote_zh: 住進去發現並沒有這回事
voices.quote_en: Once I moved in, I found there was no such thing.
voices.summary: Before moving in she heard many rumours of crime. They lived in a 5th-floor flat in a rear block that had no windows at all.
voices.source: Ming Pao Weekly (明周文化), 'Beyond the darkness: real memories of the walled city', by Leung Yi-kei, Tam Chi-wing and Wong Ka-pong, 13 June 2024

voices.name: Ping (平哥)
voices.quote_zh: 我們當年在城寨好太平
voices.quote_en: In those years in the walled city we were very peaceful.
voices.summary: He came from Chaozhou as a teenager and opened a fish-ball factory in the city in the 1980s with HK$6,000. Rent and utilities came to under HK$2,000 a month, and no licence or tax was needed. Police patrolled two or three times a day and signed a book; when a neighbour lost power, the flat above lowered a plug. After the clearance he moved the business to Fuk Lo Tsun Road.
voices.source: Ming Pao Weekly (明周文化), 'Beyond the darkness: real memories of the walled city', by Leung Yi-kei, Tam Chi-wing and Wong Ka-pong, 13 June 2024

voices.name: Former residents
voices.quote_zh: 我們在極差的處境下，擁有最美好的關係。
voices.quote_en: In such terrible conditions, we had the best relationships.
voices.summary: They remember neighbours minding each other's children so parents could work, cooking for each other, wading barefoot through the lanes when heavy rain flooded them, and keeping in touch long after the clearance.
voices.source: HKSTORY 香港故事, 'The story of Kowloon Walled City', 15 January 2025

voices.name: Members of the kaifong association
voices.summary: Young people carried water up for elderly residents for 50 cents a load; patrols walked women home at night; and the association arranged electricity meters with the power company, with residents helping to run the wiring.
voices.source: HK01, 真．城寨英雄 (series, parts 1–3), 26–28 August 2016

places.title: A dentist on Tung Tau Tsuen Road
places.sub: A ground-floor clinic on the city's north edge, 1987
places.intro: Dentists and doctors trained in mainland China, whose qualifications Hong Kong did not recognise, could practise in the walled city without fear of prosecution. Over 150 dental clinics were counted at the peak, many in a row on the road along the city's north edge. This clinic is illustrative: its name, layout and equipment are typical of a small 1980s practice, not a record of one; the facts about the city's dentists are cited where they appear.

places.sub: A ground-floor workshop inside the city, working through the night, 1987

places.title: The kaifong association office
places.sub: Where residents settled disputes and recorded sales, 1987
places.intro: No Hong Kong court or land registry reached inside, so residents ran much of the city themselves. The kaifong (neighbourhood) association grew out of a committee formed against the 1963 clearance attempt. It settled disputes, witnessed property sales on handwritten receipts, and later arranged electricity meters with the power company. This office is illustrative: its furniture and papers are typical of such an association, not a record of the real office.

places.sub: Thirteen storeys up, where the city came for air, 1987
places.intro: Above the dark lanes, the roofs were the city's open space: TV aerials, water tanks, washing lines and rubbish, linked by ladders. Children played and did homework there, adults exercised, raced pigeons, sat on bamboo chairs and watched the lights, and airliners passed low overhead on their way into Kai Tak. This rooftop is illustrative: what is on it comes from descriptions of the city's roofs, cited where they appear.

places.title: The Yamen, as a school
places.sub: The city's oldest building, among the towers, 1987
places.intro: The Yamen, the magistrate's office built in 1847, was the only building of the walled fort still standing among the towers, and the May 1987 survey labels it 'School'. Accounts describe a free school (義學) in the middle of the city, with a youth centre and an old people's centre beside it, and several schools and kindergartens in the city. This classroom is illustrative: the hall's granite and timber follow the building that survives in the park; the furniture is typical of a 1980s Hong Kong classroom.

facts.claim: The walled fort and Yamen were completed in response to British Hong Kong (Treaty of Nanking 1842)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Kowloon Walled City'

facts.claim: Features marked on the May 1987 survey: the H-shaped former Yamen labelled 'School', a clinic beside it, a temple on Tin Hau Temple Street, several shrines ('Shr'), wells ('W'), two public latrines ('Lat'), a footbridge ('FB'), an electric transformer ('ET') at the south edge, temporary structures ('TS') and a garden along the east side
In the middle stood the free school (義學, the oldest building), the youth centre and the old people's centre
